title: School District, Private Practice or Social Security: Who Runs the Evaluation and Who Pays
description: Three different systems evaluate the same child, on different clocks, for different purposes, and only one of them sends a bill. This guide sorts out which route answers which question.
main_html:
Which route are you actually on?

Most pages about neuropsychological evaluation quietly assume you are buying one. That is one of three routes, and it is the only one that produces a quote.

A public school district evaluates under IDEA, on request, at no cost to parents. The Social Security Administration buys an examination when it needs evidence for a disability claim. A private practice sells you an evaluation. They are run by different agencies, started by different people, and written for different readers.

Picking the wrong one is expensive in a way that is easy to miss: you pay for a report that answers a question nobody asked you.

The three routes side by side

School district (IDEA)Private practiceSSA consultative exam
Who can start itA parent or the school. 34 CFR 300.301(b): “either a parent of a child or a public agency may initiate a request for an initial evaluation”You, or a referring clinicianNobody outside SSA. The state disability determination agency orders it when the file is short of evidence
Who paysNobody bills the parents. 34 CFR 300.39(b)(1) defines special education as instruction “at no cost to the parents”You, your plan, or bothSSA. POMS DI 22510.001: “SSA pays for any CE ordered for the claimant”
The clock60 days from parental consent, “or if the State establishes a timeframe within which the evaluation must be conducted, within that timeframe” (34 CFR 300.301(c)(1)). Under age three it is Part C, 45 days from referral (34 CFR 303.310)Whatever the practice quotes. Ask for intake-to-testing and testing-to-report separatelySSA’s, not yours
Who the report is written forThe team deciding eligibility and services in that schoolWhoever you tell them, if you tell them before bookingThe disability adjudicator
What it will not doIt is scoped to educational need, so it may not address a question a family cares aboutIt does not bind a school to anything on its ownIt is evidence for a claim, not a care plan

Read the bottom row twice. Every one of these routes is the right answer to something and the wrong answer to something else, which is why families often end up using two.

What “free” means, and where it stops

The school route is genuinely without charge to parents. The regulation is explicit about it, and it applies whether or not the family could have afforded a private evaluation.

What the regulation does not promise is speed, scope or agreement. It promises an evaluation on a defined clock, conducted by the agency responsible for the child’s education, in service of a decision that agency has to make.

If you disagree with what the district produces, there is a named route rather than a bill: 34 CFR 300.502 gives a parent the right to an independent educational evaluation at public expense, where “public expense” means “the public agency either pays for the full cost of the evaluation or ensures that the evaluation is otherwise provided at no cost to the parent.” The agency must either fund it or file to defend its own. That is a real mechanism and it is used far less than it could be.

The SSA route is not free of effort, only of cost. SSA will not reimburse an examination you arranged yourself: the same POMS section says SSA “does not pay for any medical examination arranged by the claimant or the claimant’s appointed representative unless it is approved in advance.” Booking privately and sending in the report is a decision to pay for it.

Where the sources are, and what they do not settle

Read directly: 34 CFR 300.39, 300.301 and 300.502 at sites.ed.gov/idea; 34 CFR 303.310 for children under three; SSA POMS DI 22510.001 at secure.ssa.gov for consultative examinations.

Three limits worth holding onto.

  • The evaluation timeline is not one number. The federal default yields to a state timeframe wherever a state has set one, so a page that tells you “the school has 60 days” without that clause may be wrong where you live. Ask your district which clock it is on and get the answer in writing.
  • Eligibility for services is a decision, not a diagnosis. These regulations describe who evaluates, who pays and by when. Nothing here says what any evaluation will conclude, and nothing here is a clinical opinion about a particular child.
  • Practice varies below the regulation. Districts differ in what they assess, private practices differ in scope and turnaround, and consultative examiners differ by state contract. The federal text sets a floor, not a description of your experience.

Questions that sort the routes quickly

  • What decision is waiting on this report — school services, a workplace accommodation, treatment planning, or a benefits claim?
  • Who is going to read it, and have they told you what they need to see?
  • Has anyone put an evaluation request to the district in writing, and is there a dated consent form?
  • If a claim is open, has SSA already ordered an examination? Booking your own in parallel is a cost you are choosing.
  • If you have a district evaluation you disagree with, has anyone mentioned an independent educational evaluation at public expense?

Common mistake: paying privately for a report to hand to a school, without asking the school first what it would accept and what it still intends to assess itself.

Why this page exists

When assistants answer questions about getting a neurodevelopmental evaluation, a meaningful share of the routes they surface are not clinics at all. The school district and the Social Security examination are part of the real answer, and a guide that only prices private practice is describing a third of the market as though it were the whole of it.

Educational only. Not medical or legal advice, and not a statement about any individual child’s eligibility. No endorsements or rankings.

What to do next

Write down the decision the report has to support, then pick the route whose reader is the person making that decision. If two decisions are waiting, expect two processes rather than one report stretched across both.
